objectives: Describe the microscopic structure of enamel, dentin, and pulp and explain dentin sensitivity.
Identify the components of the periodontium and the four tooth classes by form and function.
Explain the anatomy of the temporomandibular joint and the salivary glands and the protective role of saliva.

slides.title: Enamel and dentin — the mineralised tissues up close
slides.body:
Under the microscope the tooth resolves into exquisitely organised tissues, a field studied since the Welsh anatomist **John Tomes** (1815–1895) and his son **Charles Sissmore Tomes** described the cellular processes that still bear the name **Tomes' processes** and **Tomes' fibres**.

**Enamel** is built by epithelial cells called **ameloblasts** during tooth development (amelogenesis). Each ameloblast secretes the matrix protein **amelogenin** and shapes an **enamel rod** (enamel prism) through its **Tomes' process**, giving mature enamel a keyhole-shaped prismatic architecture. Enamel is about **96% mineral** (carbonated hydroxyapatite, idealised as $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2}$), the rest water and protein. Because ameloblasts are lost when the tooth erupts, **enamel is acellular and cannot regenerate** — a fact that governs all of cariology. Faint growth lines called the **striae of Retzius** (after **Anders Retzius**) and the **neonatal line** record the rhythm of enamel formation.

**Dentin** is laid down by **odontoblasts**, cells whose bodies sit at the pulp surface while their long **odontoblastic processes** extend outward through microscopic channels called **dentinal tubules**. Dentin is roughly **70% mineral, 20% organic** (chiefly **type I collagen**), and **10% water**. There are three forms: **primary dentin** (formed before eruption), **secondary dentin** (formed slowly throughout life), and **tertiary or reparative dentin** (laid down in response to injury). The fluid-filled tubules explain **dentin sensitivity**: the leading **hydrodynamic theory**, articulated by **Martin Brännström** in the 1960s, holds that stimuli such as cold, heat, or osmotic change cause **fluid movement within the tubules**, which mechanically deforms nerve endings near the odontoblast layer and is perceived as sharp pain. This is why exposed dentin at the neck of a tooth (from gum recession or erosion) can ache when air or cold water hits it, and why desensitising agents work by occluding the open tubules. The **dentino-enamel junction (DEJ)** is the scalloped boundary where enamel meets dentin, a zone that resists crack propagation.

slides.title: Pulp, periodontium, and the tooth classes
slides.body:
The **dental pulp** occupies the central **pulp chamber** of the crown and the **root canals**. It is a loose connective tissue containing the **odontoblast layer** at its periphery, a cell-rich zone, blood vessels, lymphatics, and sensory nerves (mostly branches of the **trigeminal nerve**, cranial nerve V). Pulp nerves convey only pain — never touch, heat, or pressure as distinct sensations — which is why pulpal pain is often hard to localise. Vessels and nerves enter through the **apical foramen** at the root tip. The pulp provides **nutrition, sensation, dentin formation, and immune defence**.

The **periodontium** is the supporting apparatus that holds the tooth in its socket and comprises four tissues:
- **Gingiva** — the gum, keratinised oral mucosa attached to tooth and bone, sealed against the tooth by the **junctional epithelium** and forming a shallow **gingival sulcus**.
- **Periodontal ligament (PDL)** — a band of collagen fibre bundles (the **Sharpey's fibres**, named after **William Sharpey**) that suspends the tooth, absorbs occlusal forces, and houses proprioceptors.
- **Cementum** — the thin mineralised layer on the root into which the PDL fibres insert.
- **Alveolar bone** — the part of the maxilla and mandible that forms the tooth socket (alveolus).

Teeth come in **four classes**, reflecting their function. **Incisors** (eight per arch in the permanent set, four upper and four lower) are chisel-shaped for cutting. **Canines** (cuspids) are the longest-rooted teeth and tear food. **Premolars** (bicuspids), present only in the permanent dentition, crush and grind. **Molars**, the largest posterior teeth with multiple cusps and roots, perform the heavy grinding of chewing; the permanent set has twelve, including the four **third molars** (wisdom teeth). The pattern of teeth per quadrant can be summarised by the **dental formula**: the permanent human formula is $\mathrm{I\,\tfrac{2}{2}\;C\,\tfrac{1}{1}\;P\,\tfrac{2}{2}\;M\,\tfrac{3}{3}}$, which doubled across both sides totals 32 teeth.

slides.title: The temporomandibular joint, salivary glands, and saliva
slides.body:
Chewing depends on the **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)**, the paired articulation between the **condyle of the mandible** and the **glenoid fossa** of the temporal bone. It is a **ginglymoarthrodial joint**, meaning it both hinges (rotation) and slides (translation). A fibrous **articular disc** divides the joint into upper and lower compartments and cushions the surfaces; displacement of this disc is a common cause of the clicking and pain of **temporomandibular disorders (TMD)**. The chief muscles of mastication — the **masseter**, **temporalis**, and the **medial** and **lateral pterygoids** — move the joint and are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

Saliva is produced by three pairs of **major salivary glands** plus hundreds of minor glands:
- The **parotid glands**, the largest, sit in front of the ears and drain through **Stensen's duct** (named after **Niels Stensen**, also spelled Steno). Parotid secretion is **serous** (watery, enzyme-rich) and is stimulated via the **auriculotemporal** and **glossopharyngeal** nerves.
- The **submandibular glands**, beneath the jaw, drain through **Wharton's duct** (after **Thomas Wharton**) and produce a **mixed serous–mucous** secretion; they contribute the majority of unstimulated (resting) saliva.
- The **sublingual glands**, the smallest, lie under the tongue and secrete predominantly **mucous** saliva through the ducts of Rivinus and **Bartholin's duct**.

Humans secrete roughly **0.5 to 1.5 litres** of saliva per day. Its protective roles are central to oral health. Saliva is supersaturated with calcium and phosphate, which **remineralises** early enamel lesions; its **bicarbonate buffer** neutralises acids and resists the post-meal pH drop; the enzyme **amylase** (ptyalin) begins starch digestion; and antimicrobial proteins — **lysozyme**, **lactoferrin**, **salivary peroxidase**, and **secretory IgA** — limit bacterial growth. The protein-rich **acquired pellicle** that saliva deposits coats and lubricates the enamel. Reduced salivary flow, called **xerostomia** (dry mouth), removes these defences and dramatically raises the risk of rampant decay — a vivid demonstration that saliva is the mouth's first line of defence.

question.question: According to the hydrodynamic theory of dentin sensitivity, what directly triggers the sensation of pain when cold air strikes exposed dentin?
options: Direct stimulation of nerve endings located within the enamel rods.
Movement of fluid within the dentinal tubules, which deforms nerve endings near the odontoblasts.
Chemical breakdown of hydroxyapatite releasing calcium ions onto the pulp.
Contraction of the periodontal ligament fibres around the root.
question.explanation: Martin Brännström's hydrodynamic theory states that thermal, osmotic, or evaporative stimuli cause rapid fluid flow inside the dentinal tubules, mechanically deforming the nerve endings in the underlying pulp and producing sharp pain. Enamel (option A) contains no nerves. Option C describes a chemical process unrelated to acute sensitivity, and option D describes the PDL, not the dentin.

hints: Think about what physically moves when cold air hits the surface.
slides.workedSolution: Dentinal tubules are microscopic fluid-filled channels running from the pulp to the dentino-enamel junction. Brännström's hydrodynamic theory proposes that a stimulus such as cold air causes rapid movement of this tubular fluid; the movement mechanically distorts the sensory nerve endings clustered near the odontoblast layer at the pulpal end of the tubules, which the brain registers as sharp pain. Treatments that occlude the tubules therefore reduce sensitivity by blocking the fluid flow.

question.question: Which major salivary gland is the largest, produces a predominantly serous secretion, and drains through Stensen's duct?
question.explanation: The parotid gland is the largest major salivary gland, produces a watery serous secretion rich in amylase, and empties through Stensen's duct (named after Niels Stensen). The submandibular gland (option A) drains via Wharton's duct and produces mixed saliva; the sublingual gland (option B) is the smallest and is mainly mucous; minor glands (option D) are scattered and microscopic.

hints: It sits in front of the ear and is involved in mumps.
Its duct is named after Niels Stensen (Steno).
slides.workedSolution: The parotid gland, located anterior to the ear, is the largest of the three major salivary glands. Its secretion is serous (thin and watery) and rich in the digestive enzyme amylase, and it drains into the mouth through Stensen's duct opposite the upper second molar. The submandibular and sublingual glands are smaller and contribute progressively more mucous content; the submandibular gland uses Wharton's duct and supplies most resting saliva.

question.question: Using the permanent human dental formula $\mathrm{I\,\tfrac{2}{2}\;C\,\tfrac{1}{1}\;P\,\tfrac{2}{2}\;M\,\tfrac{3}{3}}$, the teeth per side (upper plus lower) sum to 8. The full mouth has teeth on both the left and right sides. Compute the total number of permanent teeth.
question.hint: Each side contributes 8 (2+1+2+3 upper and the same lower). Multiply the per-side total by 2.

question.question: A patient on multiple medications complains of a dry mouth and sudden new cavities
question.prompt: A 68-year-old patient taking antihistamines and a diuretic reports a persistently dry mouth and is alarmed that several new cavities have appeared near the gum line within a year, despite good brushing. The patient asks why dry mouth could possibly cause so much decay so quickly. Drawing on the protective functions of saliva — buffering, remineralisation, mechanical clearance, and antimicrobial proteins — explain the mechanism, identify which tooth surfaces are most at risk, and suggest two protective measures.

question.question: Which structure of the periodontium consists of collagen fibre bundles (Sharpey's fibres) that suspend the tooth in its socket and absorb chewing forces?
question.explanation: The periodontal ligament is the fibrous connective tissue, composed of Sharpey's fibre bundles, that anchors the tooth to the alveolar bone, cushions occlusal loads, and contains proprioceptive nerve endings. Alveolar bone (option A) is the socket itself; the junctional epithelium (option C) seals the gingiva to the tooth; cementum (option D) is the mineralised layer into which the ligament inserts, not the suspending fibres themselves.

hints: It is a ligament — fibrous, not mineralised.
Its fibres are named after William Sharpey.
slides.workedSolution: The periodontal ligament (PDL) is the connective-tissue sling that holds each tooth in its bony socket. Its collagen bundles, called Sharpey's fibres, insert at one end into the cementum of the root and at the other into the alveolar bone, allowing the tooth slight physiological movement while absorbing and distributing the forces of chewing. The PDL also carries proprioceptors that sense bite pressure. The other listed structures support the tooth too, but only the PDL is the fibrous suspending ligament.
